title: Judgment Engines
lines: Judgment Engines examines the systems that decide whether other outputs are good enough.
Those decisions can shape rewards, selection, and institutional actions without appearing in the final interface.
The book argues that a reliable judge is an engineered procedure, not merely a model prompt.
It connects rubrics and evaluation methods with evidence, security, calibration, and accountable authority.
Readers learn to distinguish a repeatable score from a judgment that measures the intended quality.
The central requirement is that an automated evaluator must itself remain open to evaluation and challenge.

title: Evaluation becomes an action
lines: A judgment may rank candidates, trigger revision, shape training, or permit a consequential action.
Those uses turn evaluation into part of the system's behavior.
The book therefore separates what is assessed from the norms governing its assessment.
It also distinguishes the procedure from the authority attached to the result.
A score can be reproducible while expressing the wrong standard for its purpose.
This foundation explains why better prompting alone cannot settle the engineering problem.

title: Make the standard visible
lines: Different judgments require different forms, including comparison, critique, grading, or a veto.
An explicit rubric states the qualities the evaluator is supposed to recognize.
Without that definition, apparently precise scores can conceal an unstable meaning of quality.
The book examines how criteria become instructions, examples, and evidence requirements.
A rubric still needs testing because clear wording does not guarantee valid measurement.
Readers gain a vocabulary for discussing disagreement before averaging it into a single number.

title: Build the procedure
lines: The engineering chapters follow a candidate through a complete evaluation procedure.
Candidate material is untrusted input, even when it contains persuasive instructions to the judge.
Trusted criteria, evidence retrieval, tool execution, and consequence policies need separate responsibilities.
A panel of judges can add perspectives without providing independent evidence automatically.
Shared models or assumptions may make their errors strongly related.
The book turns the idea of a judge into a system whose failure points can be inspected.

title: Agreement is not validity
lines: Two evaluators can agree consistently and still assess the wrong thing.
Repeatability concerns stability, while validity concerns the quality the judgment is intended to measure.
Calibration asks another question about how confidence relates to observed correctness.
The book uses these distinctions to organize evaluation of evaluators themselves.
Bias tests and changing task conditions can reveal weaknesses hidden by overall agreement.
This is the point where a convenient scoring tool becomes a demanding measurement problem.

title: The judge can be targeted
lines: An evaluated answer may try to influence the procedure deciding its quality.
Instruction injection and reward gaming therefore belong inside the book's account of judgment.
Evidence checking must also distinguish an asserted tool result from an actual execution.
For agents, the evaluation may need to inspect trajectories rather than final answers alone.
The surrounding system determines what evidence is available and what actions a verdict permits.
Readers can use these chapters to locate the boundary between evaluation data and evaluator authority.

title: Different domains, different stakes
lines: The applications move across science, software, education, professional review, and other consequential settings.
Their variety does not imply that one universal rubric should govern every domain.
Some judgments require plural standards, specialist evidence, or an explicit capacity to abstain.
Aesthetic evaluation makes the limits of one supposedly neutral score especially visible.
The book uses these differences to test its architecture against more than one convenient benchmark.
Its reader gains come from comparing requirements rather than copying a verdict between unrelated contexts.

title: Who can challenge a score
lines: The institutional chapters ask what happens when someone contests an automated evaluation.
A recorded reason matters only if the surrounding policy permits meaningful reconsideration.
The book connects appeals, abstention, oversight, and continuing measurement with technical design.
It also asks who evaluates the institutions that install and maintain the judges.
These questions prevent accountability from shrinking into a dashboard of internal performance scores.
The central argument returns here: the evaluator must remain visible to evaluation itself.

title: Read before granting authority
lines: Start by identifying the consequence attached to a judge's output.
Read the chapters on norms and rubrics before choosing an evaluation model.
Then follow the procedure, measurement, and security chapters as one connected design problem.
The later institutional discussion asks whether the resulting authority can be challenged in practice.
Judgment Engines is worth reading when evaluation quietly begins to govern real decisions.
It helps distinguish a useful assistant to judgment from an unchecked source of institutional power.
